item.title: Arita Ceramics Fair — Guide
item.description: The Arita Ceramics Fair (Arita Toki-ichi), held every year during Golden Week (roughly 29 April–5 May), is the largest and most famous pottery market in Japan. For a week, the main street of the historic porcelain town of Arita — birthplace of Japanese porcelain — is lined for some four kilometres with hundreds of stalls, as kilns, wholesalers and shops sell everything from everyday tableware to fine art pieces, often at significant discounts and bargain prices.

item.title: Arita: Birthplace of Japanese Porcelain — Guide
item.description: Arita is the birthplace of Japanese porcelain, where the first true porcelain in Japan was fired in the early 1600s after kaolin clay was discovered nearby. For over four centuries the town has produced Arita-yaki (also known as Imari ware), refined white porcelain painted in cobalt blue and vivid overglaze colours, exported around the world and prized to this day. The town is a living museum of ceramics: porcelain museums display masterpieces old and new, historic kilns and shops line the streets, and Tozan Shrine, the potters' guardian, is famous for its unique torii gate, lanterns and railings all made of blue-and-white porcelain.

item.title: Imari and Its Porcelain Park — Guide
item.description: Imari gave its name to the porcelain — ‘Imari ware’ — that was shipped from its port to Europe from the seventeenth century, though most was actually made in nearby Arita and the secret Nabeshima kilns of Okawachiyama. Today the area celebrates this heritage, and one of its more unusual attractions is the Imari Okawachiyama Porcelain Park, a spacious theme park built around a striking full-scale replica of a German baroque palace (Zwinger Palace), reflecting the historic ties between Arita porcelain and European royal collections.

item.title: Noritake Garden: Porcelain Craft in a Red-Brick Park — Guide
item.description: Noritake Garden occupies the site of the original 1904 works of Noritake, the porcelain maker whose fine tableware graced dinner tables worldwide, and turns the old factory grounds into a leafy urban park framed by red-brick workshops and the chimney stubs of former kilns. The craft centre is the heart of the visit: you watch artisans shape, fire and hand-paint porcelain at every stage, browse a museum of the company’s dazzling early ‘Old Noritake’ art pieces, and can even paint your own design onto a plate before browsing the outlet shop’s tableware bargains.
